name: Virtual Hosts - Brute Force
description: Different vhosts can serve entirely different sites from the same IP by varying the Host header. Brute-force the Host header to find hidden virtual hosts.

defense.why_it_works: Virtual host brute-forcing sends HTTP requests with different `Host:` header values to discover additional websites hosted on the same IP. Web servers using name-based virtual hosting return different content per `Host:` header, exposing admin panels, development sites, or internal applications not linked publicly.
defense.prerequisites: A target IP/host known to serve name-based virtual hosts, and a wordlist of candidate host names.
defense.impact: Uncovers additional sites served from the same IP (admin panels, internal apps, staging) that don't resolve in public DNS — expanding the attack surface behind a single address.
defense.detection:
Virtual host discovery can generate significant traffic and might be detected by intrusion detection systems (IDS) or web application firewalls (WAF). High-volume requests to a single IP with rapidly changing Host header values are a clear indicator of vhost scanning — this pattern is abnormal for legitimate browser traffic.

[MITRE T1595.003 M1056] Monitor for suspicious network traffic that could indicate scanning, such as network packets with anomalous amounts of web server interactions exhibiting unusual or automated characteristics.
defense.artifacts: High-rate HTTP requests to one IP with varying Host headers appear in web server logs and commonly trigger WAF/IDS signatures.
defense.prevention:
Configure web servers to return a generic 404 response for unrecognized Host headers rather than defaulting to any application. Deploy WAF rules to detect and block Host-header fuzzing (high-rate requests with varied Host values). Implement rate limiting per source IP at the web server or load balancer layer.

[MITRE T1595.003 M1056] This technique cannot be easily mitigated with preventive controls since it is based on behaviors performed outside enterprise defenses. Efforts should focus on minimizing the amount and sensitivity of data available to external parties.
defense.evasion: Throttle the request rate to stay below WAF/IDS thresholds. Use realistic user-agent strings and add jitter between requests to mimic legitimate browser traffic.
defense.misconfiguration: Web application and infrastructure information is inadvertently exposed: verbose HTTP headers (Server, X-Powered-By) revealing exact version numbers, directory listing enabled on web servers, .git repositories or .env files accessible in the web root, robots.txt listing sensitive paths, and WHOIS data exposing internal contact details.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Apache with version disclosure in headers:
# HTTP response: Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
# X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3  <-- exact version, enables targeted exploit search

# Directory listing enabled:
# nginx: autoindex on;  <- any directory without index.html lists files
# Apache: Options +Indexes

# .git accessible from web root:
# http://target.com/.git/config  -- exposes repo + credentials in config
# http://target.com/.env  -- exposes DB_PASSWORD, API keys
defense.secure_config:
# Apache — remove version disclosure:
# /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/security.conf:
ServerTokens Prod          # shows only 'Apache' not version
ServerSignature Off        # removes version from error pages

# nginx:
server_tokens off;         # hides nginx version

# Disable directory listing:
# Apache: Options -Indexes
# nginx: remove 'autoindex on' from all location blocks

# Block sensitive files/directories:
# Apache:
<DirectoryMatch '(\.git|\.env|\.svn|backup|config)'>
    Require all denied
</DirectoryMatch>

# nginx:
location ~* /(\.git|\.env|\.svn|backup\/) { deny all; return 404; }

# Remove X-Powered-By header:
# PHP: expose_php = Off (php.ini)
